newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Election, what election? grumble Euro-MPs.
newsitem.headline: Election, what election? grumble Euro-MPs.

text.p: When the European Parliament elects its new president on Tuesday in Strasbourg it knows there is only one man for the job -- Spaniard Jose-Maria Gil-Robles-- after a deal between the assembly's two big political groups.

One woman, France's Catherine Lalumiere, intends to challenge that fait accompli, responding to wide criticism that the carve-up amounts to an undemocratic cartel between the EU's big political and national powers to the exclusion of the small.

Under a long-standing deal cooked up between the biggest group the Socialists and the second biggest, the Christian Democratic European People's Party (EPP), each holds half of the presidency during the five-year legislature.
The horse trading did not stop there.

The choice of the EPP president who will chair the assembly as it seeks new powers in the closing stages of the EU's intergovernmental conference, came down to a deal between its two biggest national delegations Germany and Spain.
German Egon Klepsch was selected five years ago, meaning it was Spain's turn to enjoy the prestige of the presidency.
The arrangement ruled out Gil-Robles' two EPP challengers -- France's Nicole Fontaine, sponsored by French President Jacques Chirac, and Greece's Georgios Anastassopoulos.

A group of 10 leading French women, including French European Commissioner and former prime minister Edith Cresson and Lalumiere herself said in a joint statement the process had robbed the Parliament of an authoritative and experienced woman president -- in Fontaine.
They denounced the move saying it was in contradition to the EU policy of strengthening the role of women voluntarily rather than through quotas.

Lalumiere, former Secretary General of the Council of Europe and leader of the Parliament's alternative European Radical Alliance, said she was entering the race as the procedure "excludes the small member states, then the small parties then the small delegations within large groups."
She said the carve-up sapped the credibility of the EU's directly-elected assembly, which is trying to justify its demands for more powers on democratic grounds.
Parliamentary officials said she could clock up around 100 of the parliament's 626 votes, in a protest vote which could extend to the disillusioned in the bigger parties too.
Liberal leader Gijs De Vries said his group would back Lalumiere and that the president should be elected and not selected.
Green leader Claudia Roth said Lalumiere was more than a symbolic candidate and that all the arguments were for her.
Lalumiere had international and European experience through her work as a minister and Secretary General of the Council of Europe and it was time to have a woman president.
"After years and years and years of a man, it would be a good thing to have a woman," she said.

The backstage division of top jobs also extends to the positions of vice president, the five quaestors who oversee deputies' interests and spending, and the chairmanship of more than 20 parliamentary committees, which scrutinise and amend draft EU legislation.
